name: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
definition: A long-term digestive condition with repeated abdominal pain and changes in bowel habit, but no visible damage or disease in the digestive tract.
overview: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common long-term condition of the digestive system. It causes stomach cramps, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation, and these symptoms tend to come and go. The NHS says it is usually a lifelong problem, although changes to diet and lifestyle and medicines can help. The exact cause is unknown. MedlinePlus says it affects about twice as many women as men and is most often found in people younger than 45.
causes: It has been linked to food moving through the gut too quickly or too slowly.
It has been linked to oversensitive nerves in the gut.
Experts think problems with brain-gut interaction may play a part.
Stress and a family history of IBS have also been linked to it.
riskFactors: Gastroenteritis has been suggested as a link, although none of the proposed links is proven
Being female: about twice as many women as men are affected
Flare-up triggers include alcohol, caffeine, spicy or fatty foods, stress and anxiety, and regular antibiotic use
signs: Often no visible sign of damage or disease in the digestive tract
Examination looks for warning features such as anaemia or abdominal or rectal masses, which prompt further investigation
complications: Pain can be troublesome, but IBS does not damage the digestive tract
A survey found people with IBS reported more worry and anxiety about diet than people without IBS
diagnosis: There is no test that confirms IBS. A doctor can usually diagnose it from the typical symptoms. Tests are used to rule out other conditions. A GP may arrange a blood test for coeliac disease and stool tests for infection or inflammatory bowel disease. NICE guidance says a diagnosis of IBS should be considered only if there is abdominal pain or discomfort. Assessment includes looking for red flag features, and a positive diagnosis can be made once these and other causes such as coeliac disease are ruled out.
treatment: Diet and lifestyle changes are the first step, and medicines can often help control symptoms. Medicines depend on the main symptom: antispasmodics or peppermint oil for pain and bloating, loperamide for diarrhoea, and fibre or short-term laxatives for constipation. Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants are sometimes used for pain. Cognitive behavioural therapy and hypnotherapy are other options. A GP may refer to a dietitian, who may suggest a low FODMAP diet.
prevention: The NHS lists alcohol, caffeine, spicy or fatty foods, stress and anxiety and regular antibiotic use as triggers of flare-ups. A food and symptom diary, enough fluid, regular exercise and stress management are described as self-help measures.
seekCare: A routine GP appointment is advised when IBS may be the cause and symptoms have lasted more than 4 weeks. An urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 is advised for unexplained weight loss, bleeding from the rectum or bloody diarrhoea, a hard lump or swelling in the tummy, or breathlessness, palpitations or unusually pale skin.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of IBS?
sections.body:
The main symptoms of IBS are stomach pain or cramps, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation. Some people have mostly diarrhoea, some mostly constipation, and some have both. The NHS says symptoms tend to come and go, and an episode can last for days, weeks or months at a time. Other symptoms the NHS lists include wind, passing mucus with stools, tiredness and a lack of energy, feeling sick, backache, urinary problems, bowel incontinence and pelvic pain.

NIDDK adds that a feeling of not having finished a bowel movement, and whitish mucus in the stool, can occur. It also says women with IBS often have more symptoms during their periods. IBS can be painful, but NIDDK says it does not damage the digestive tract. Because the symptoms overlap with those of coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease, doctors consider those conditions too.

sections.heading: What causes IBS and what triggers flare-ups?
sections.body:
The NHS says the exact cause of IBS is not known. It has been linked to food moving through the gut too quickly or too slowly, oversensitive nerves in the gut, stress and a family history of IBS. NIDDK says experts think a combination of problems may lead to IBS, and that different factors may cause it in different people. One proposed mechanism is a problem with brain-gut interaction, which may change how fast food moves through the digestive tract. Proposed links also include a bout of gastroenteritis, although NHS inform says none has been proven to lead to IBS.

Flare-ups can happen for no obvious reason, the NHS says. The common triggers it lists are alcohol, caffeine, spicy or fatty foods, stress and anxiety, and regular use of antibiotics. Keeping a food and symptom diary is one way described to spot personal triggers.

sections.heading: How is IBS diagnosed?
sections.body:
There is no single test for IBS, and doctors mostly rely on the pattern of symptoms. NICE guidance says a diagnosis of IBS should be considered only if there is abdominal pain or discomfort. Doctors examine for red flag features, such as rectal bleeding, unexplained weight loss, anaemia, or lumps in the abdomen or rectum. If any are present, NICE says the person should be referred for further investigation.

Tests are used mainly to rule out other conditions. A GP may order a blood test for coeliac disease and stool tests for infection or inflammatory bowel disease. NICE says a stool test for faecal calprotectin, alongside clinical assessment, may help tell suspected inflammatory bowel disease from conditions without inflammation of the bowel. Once warning features and other causes such as coeliac disease are ruled out, a positive diagnosis of IBS can be made. NIDDK notes that IBS shows no visible signs of damage or disease in the digestive tract.

sections.heading: How is IBS treated?
sections.body:
The NHS describes lifestyle measures as the first step, with medicines added for symptoms that persist. Self-help includes a healthy balanced diet, drinking enough fluid, managing stress and exercising regularly. NICE says healthcare professionals should review fibre intake, and that insoluble fibre such as bran should be discouraged. If symptoms persist, a GP may refer someone to a dietitian, who may suggest a low FODMAP diet. NIDDK describes FODMAPs as carbohydrates that are hard to digest.

Choice of medicine depends on the main symptom. Antispasmodics can ease abdominal pain, peppermint oil can help bloating and pain, and loperamide can treat diarrhoea. Fibre supplements or short-term laxatives can help constipation. Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants are sometimes used for pain. Cognitive behavioural therapy and hypnotherapy are also options, and NIDDK says CBT has been linked with better symptom severity and quality of life.

sections.heading: Who gets IBS and when should it be checked by a doctor?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says IBS is common, affects about twice as many women as men, and is most often found in people younger than 45. The NHS advises a non-urgent GP appointment if IBS may be the cause and symptoms have lasted more than 4 weeks.

An urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 is advised for unexplained weight loss, bleeding from the rectum or bloody diarrhoea, a hard lump or swelling in the tummy, or breathlessness, palpitations or unusually pale skin. Several similar features, such as rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia and abdominal masses, are the ones clinicians check for before making a diagnosis of IBS. NHS inform also lists a change in bowel habit lasting over six weeks, especially after age 50, as a reason to see a GP urgently.

faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for IBS and that it is usually a lifelong problem. Symptoms tend to come and go, and changes to diet and lifestyle, together with medicines, can often help control them. Psychological treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy and hypnotherapy are also options for some people.

faqs.q: Is IBS the same as inflammatory bowel disease?
faqs.a: No, they are described as different conditions, although their symptoms can overlap. Doctors may use blood and stool tests to help tell them apart. NIDDK says IBS shows no visible signs of damage or disease in the digestive tract. NICE says faecal calprotectin may help distinguish suspected inflammatory bowel disease from non-inflammatory bowel disease.

NIDDK says IBS can be painful but does not damage the digestive tract. Doctors still look for warning features, such as rectal bleeding, unexplained weight loss or anaemia. When these are present, NICE says the person should be referred for further investigation.

The NHS lists stress among the factors linked to IBS, and says stress and anxiety can trigger flare-ups. NHS inform says none of the proposed causes has been proven to lead to IBS. The exact cause is unknown, and NIDDK says different factors may cause IBS in different people.

The NHS lists alcohol, caffeine, and spicy or fatty foods as common triggers. A food and symptom diary is described as a way to spot personal triggers. If symptoms persist, a GP may refer someone to a dietitian, who may suggest a low FODMAP diet.
